5635.title: Probabilistic Robotics
5635.heading: Probabilistic Robotics
5635.content:
Probabilistic robotics represents uncertain states, sensors, movements, and actions with probability distributions. Rather than committing prematurely to one world state, a robot updates competing hypotheses as evidence and controls arrive.

Localization, sensor fusion, behavior recognition, and decision models share this foundation. Their descriptions differ, but each makes incompleteness explicit and asks an inference question suited to the task.

5638.title: Probabilistic Occlusion
5638.heading: Probabilistic Occlusion
5638.content:
Probabilistic occlusion represents uncertainty about whether a real or virtual surface is in front instead of forcing every pixel into a perfectly known binary decision. Tracking error, model error, and uncertain boundaries can all contribute to the probability.

The composite can use that uncertainty to soften or otherwise manage ambiguous regions. This avoids presenting an inaccurate hard edge as if the registration and scene model were exact.

5641.title: Probabilistic Model
5641.heading: Probabilistic Model
5641.content:
A probabilistic model represents knowledge about variables and their relationships with a joint probability distribution. It makes uncertainty explicit and supports conditional questions when observations do not determine one certain conclusion.

The model is defined by its chosen variables, dependencies, forms, and parameters. Inference may be mathematically correct while the answer remains unsuitable if those modeling choices omit a relationship important to the phenomenon.

5643.sourceSearchName: probabilistic model based clustering probabilistic model based clustering

5644.sourceSearchName: probabilistic model based clustering probabilistic model based clustering
5644.title: Probabilistic Model-Based Clustering
5644.heading: Probabilistic Model-Based Clustering
5644.content:
Model-based clustering assumes observations were generated by a mixture of probability distributions whose component memberships are unknown. Each component represents a cluster with estimable parameters.

The analyst fits the model by maximizing likelihood and can compare competing component counts or covariance structures. The result supports overlapping, probability-weighted memberships rather than only hard assignments.

5647.title: Probabilistic Diagnosis
5647.heading: Probabilistic Diagnosis
5647.content:
Probabilistic diagnosis infers hidden causes from observed effects. A generative description specifies how candidate causes produce evidence, and a Bayesian question reverses that relationship through conditioning and marginalization.

No separate inverse model is required when the joint description is available. Priors distinguish explanations that fit the same observation but were not equally plausible beforehand.

5650.heading: Probabilistic Clustering Membership
5650.content:
Probabilistic clustering membership assigns each observation a distribution over clusters, so its membership values sum to one. Increasing membership in one group necessarily reduces the amount available to the others.

When interpreted as fuzzy degrees, this formulation remains fundamentally partition-oriented. It represents uncertainty about assignment among alternatives.

5653.title: Probabilistic Control
5653.heading: Probabilistic Control
5653.content:
Probabilistic control infers actions that make a desired state or observation plausible under an uncertain system model. It treats action as a searched variable while goals and available evidence condition the question.

The answer can retain a distribution over actions instead of pretending one command is certainly correct. This makes ambiguity, sensor uncertainty, and uncertain dynamics explicit in the controller's choice.

5656.sourceSearchName: probabilistic classification accuracy probabilistic classification accuracy
5656.title: Probabilistic Classification Accuracy
5656.heading: Probabilistic Classification Accuracy
5656.content:
Probabilistic classification accuracy evaluates predicted class probabilities without immediately discarding them through a fixed decision threshold. Proper scoring rules reward probability assigned to the observed class and penalize confident errors more strongly.

Threshold-based measures can still be derived for operational decisions, but probability-sensitive evaluation asks whether confidence is informative as well as whether the top-ranked label is correct.

5659.title: Proactive Assistant
5659.heading: Proactive Assistant
5659.content:
A proactive assistant initiates a suggestion, warning, or action based on predicted user needs and changing context. It may use schedules, location, external events, and prior behavior to decide when help could be valuable.

Proactivity increases utility but also the risk of interruption, mistaken inference, and unwanted surveillance. The assistant needs conservative policies and transparent control over the [[Personal Context]] it uses.

5662.sourceSearchName: proactive ai ethics proactive ai ethics
5662.title: Proactive AI Ethics
5662.heading: Proactive AI Ethics
5662.content:
Proactive AI ethics considers moral and social consequences during research, design, and policy formation rather than waiting for a widely deployed system to cause harm. Early work can influence goals, data practices, architecture, and whether an application should proceed at all.

Forecasting is imperfect because new technologies have unintended and context-dependent effects. Concrete scenarios, stakeholder participation, staged testing, and continued monitoring help without pretending the future is fully knowable. Proactivity is therefore an iterative responsibility: anticipate what can be anticipated, preserve the ability to revise, and avoid making harmful infrastructure difficult to reverse.

5665.sourceSearchName: privacy utility tradeoff privacy utility tradeoff
5665.title: Privacy-Utility Tradeoff
5665.heading: Privacy-Utility Tradeoff
5665.content:
Privacy-preserving analysis often reduces the detail available about an individual while retaining useful population-level evidence. In the book's randomized-response example, some survey answers are deliberately obscured by a secret coin flip, yet the proportion of true answers can be estimated across the group.

More noise can strengthen protection but reduce analytical precision. Differential-privacy methods formalize this tension for data collection and queries. Keeping source data on participating devices, as in federated learning, changes a different part of the tradeoff: raw records need not be centralized, although shared model updates still require privacy scrutiny.

5668.title: Private Cloud
5668.heading: Private Cloud
5668.content:
A private cloud restricts its services to a single person, organizational unit, or enterprise. It normally delivers those services over a local or wide-area private network, though access may also cross the Internet through strong restrictions.

The model gives the owning entity greater control over security, performance, and data location than a general public service. That control can require greater capital, operational expertise, and responsibility for keeping the cloud's automation and measurement capabilities working.

5671.sourceSearchName: privacy by design privacy by design
5671.title: Privacy by Design
5671.heading: Privacy by Design
5671.content:
Privacy by design makes privacy a requirement throughout the engineering process rather than a feature added after data practices are fixed. It can influence collection limits, default settings, access control, retention, combination, user information, and the ability to erase or correct data.

The approach is especially important for AI because models often depend on large datasets and may infer information beyond what was directly supplied. General commitments must be translated into concrete decisions about purpose and risk. [[Meaningful Digital Consent]] remains important, but privacy-preserving defaults reduce the burden placed on individuals to understand every technical consequence.

Kelleher and Tierney use children's free-to-play games with third-party advertising to show why privacy cannot be delegated to a downstream provider or considered only after launch. Designers must inspect the users, the records shared with advertising networks, and the content those networks return. Privacy by design makes those consequences part of the system's initial architecture and organizational practice.

5674.content:
Privacy-preserving feature selection identifies useful variables while limiting disclosure about sensitive samples or features. Mechanisms may perturb statistics, distribute computation, or provide formal privacy guarantees.

Privacy changes the evaluation problem because exact relevance scores can themselves leak information. The method must balance predictive utility, selection reliability, computational cost, and the strength of protection.

5677.heading: Privacy by Default
5677.content:
Privacy by default configures a system so that a person receives meaningful privacy protection without having to discover and change permissive settings. Only data needed for the stated purpose should be collected, exposed, retained, or made broadly accessible by default.

The approach complements [[Privacy by Design]] by turning an architectural commitment into the initial behavior experienced by users.

5680.heading: Privacy as a Secondary Rule
5680.content:
Privacy as a secondary rule treats privacy as a constraint on how legal powers are recognized, changed, and applied. It does not operate only as a primary command telling particular actors not to disclose information.

This view makes privacy part of the architecture of legitimate governance. In data-intensive societies, it limits the reach of observation and decision systems so that legal subjects retain the autonomy needed to participate in the legal order.

5683.title: Priority Setting in AI Ethics
5683.heading: Priority Setting in AI Ethics
5683.content:
Priority setting in AI ethics asks how attention, money, policy, and technical effort should be allocated among AI risks and other urgent social or environmental problems. The severity of a possible harm, the quality of evidence, the time horizon, and the opportunity cost of action all matter.

Speculative danger from future superintelligence may be grave but uncertain, while discrimination and surveillance are already present. AI itself may also distract from poverty, war, or climate change unless it contributes to addressing them. Ethical priority setting makes these comparisons explicit rather than allowing technological novelty or powerful institutions to define urgency by default.

5689.heading: Principle of Moments
5689.content: The principle of moments states that an object in rotational equilibrium has zero resultant moment about any point. In planar problems, the sum of clockwise moments equals the sum of counterclockwise moments. Complete static equilibrium also requires zero [[Resultant Force]], because balanced torques alone do not prevent translation.

5692.title: Prior Probability
5692.heading: Prior Probability
5692.content:
Prior probability represents knowledge about a variable or parameter before the selected evidence is incorporated. It is part of the broader preliminary knowledge encoded by the modeler, not the whole of Bayesian modeling.

The prior combines with a likelihood to produce a posterior. When later data arrives sequentially, the previous posterior can serve as the next prior, preserving the information accumulated so far.

The principle of least privilege gives each process or user only the permissions needed for its current task. Limiting authority confines the damage possible from errors, misuse, or compromise.

Privileges should be narrow in scope and duration rather than granted permanently for convenience. Applying the principle requires understanding actual workflows so restrictions do not force unsafe workarounds.

5701.heading: Principal Ideal
5701.content:
A principal ideal is generated by one element. In a commutative ring it consists of all multiples of that generator and is written ⟨a⟩.

The book uses principal ideals in polynomial rings to describe kernels of evaluation maps and construct quotient fields.

5704.heading: Principal Ideal in a One-Variable Polynomial Ring
5704.content:
Every ideal in K[x], where K is a [[Field]], is generated by one polynomial. Choosing a nonzero element of least degree and applying the [[Polynomial Division Algorithm]] shows that every other ideal element has zero remainder on division by it.

Thus K[x] is a principal ideal domain. This property supports polynomial greatest-common-divisor and Bézout calculations.

5707.title: Principal Component
5707.heading: Principal Component
5707.content:
A principal component is a linear combination of centered variables defining a direction of variation in a dataset. The first component has the greatest possible variance among unit-length directions, and each later component is orthogonal to the earlier ones while maximizing remaining variance.

Sample coordinates along these directions are called component scores. A component is a mathematical combination of features and requires loadings, scores, and experimental metadata for substantive interpretation.

5710.title: Principal Component Analysis
5710.heading: Principal Component Analysis
5710.content:
Principal component analysis rotates centered multivariate data into orthogonal [[Principal Component|principal components]] ordered by decreasing variance. Keeping the leading components yields a linear [[Dimension Reduction]] that captures the dominant directions of variation.

The source connects PCA directly to [[Singular Value Decomposition]] and uses component plots to examine sample relationships and batch structure. Components reveal variation, but experimental context determines whether that variation is biological, technical, or irrelevant.

For visual feature engineering, PCA can compress high-dimensional image descriptors into orthogonal coordinates that preserve as much variance as possible. It is a linear latent representation, so curved manifold structure may require nonlinear alternatives.

5713.heading: Prime Ideals Under Localization
5713.content:
The [[Prime Ideal]]s of S⁻¹R correspond exactly to prime ideals of R that are disjoint from the [[Multiplicatively Closed Set]] S. A source prime extends to a localized prime, and contracting returns the original prime.

Any prime meeting S becomes the whole localized ring because it contains an element made invertible. This correspondence explains why localization restricts the spectrum to primes compatible with the chosen denominators.

5716.title: Prime Ideal
5716.heading: Prime Ideal
5716.content:
A proper [[Ideal]] p is prime when ab ∈ p implies a ∈ p or b ∈ p. Equivalently, the [[Quotient Ring]] R/p is an [[Integral Domain]].

Prime ideals form the points of the [[Spectrum of a Ring]]. They also control radicals, localization, dimension, and primary decomposition. Every [[Maximal Ideal]] is prime because a field is an integral domain.

The source proves the quotient characterization alongside maximal ideals: a proper ideal is prime exactly when its quotient has no zero divisors. This supplies a structural test that avoids checking the product condition directly.

5719.heading: Prime Ideal Height
5719.content:
The height ht(p) of a [[Prime Ideal]] p is the supremum of lengths of strict prime chains ending at p. It measures the dimension below that point of the spectrum.

The Krull height theorem bounds the height of each minimal prime over an ideal generated by n elements by n. Localization at p preserves this height as the dimension of the local ring R_p.

5725.heading: Prime Avoidance Theorem
5725.content:
The prime avoidance theorem states that if an [[Ideal]] is contained in a finite union of [[Prime Ideal]]s, then it is contained in one of them. The finite union cannot cover the ideal only by distributing different elements among different primes.

A dual intersection statement says that if a prime contains a finite intersection of ideals, then it contains at least one of those ideals. These forms help select elements outside specified primes.

5728.title: Prime Characteristic
5728.heading: Prime Characteristic
5728.content:
A nontrivial integral domain with positive characteristic must have prime characteristic. If the characteristic factored, the corresponding nonzero multiples of the identity would multiply to zero.

Finite fields therefore have prime characteristic even when their number of elements is a higher prime power.

5731.title: Primary Submodule
5731.heading: Primary Submodule
5731.content:
A proper submodule N of a finitely generated module M is primary when rm ∈ N with m ∉ N forces a positive power of r to send all of M into N.

The radical of the ideal (N:M) is a [[Prime Ideal]] p, and N is called p-primary. The quotient M/N is then a [[Primary Module]].

5734.title: Primary Key
5734.heading: Primary Key
5734.content:
A primary key is a column or combination of columns whose value uniquely identifies each row in a [[Relational Database|relational database]] table. The database management system rejects changes that would create two rows with the same key.

Key uniqueness also guarantees that no two table rows are identical, preserving the mathematical interpretation of a table as a set of tuples rather than a collection with duplicates.

5737.title: Primary Module
5737.heading: Primary Module
5737.content:
An R-module M is p-primary when its set of associated primes is exactly {p}. Its zero divisors are therefore controlled by one [[Prime Ideal]].

For a Noetherian module, p-primary behavior can be characterized through injection into M_p together with annihilation of each element by some power of p. Primary modules are the quotient pieces arising from [[Primary Submodule]]s.

5740.title: Primary Ideal
5740.heading: Primary Ideal
5740.content:
A proper ideal q is primary when xy ∈ q and x ∉ q imply that some positive power of y belongs to q. Equivalently, every [[Zero Divisor]] in R/q is [[Nilpotent Element|nilpotent]].

The radical √q of a primary ideal is a [[Prime Ideal]]. Primary ideals act like prime powers in a decomposition, retaining multiplicity information that a radical alone discards.

Defining it during concept development forces the proposal to describe the actual experience rather than only its setting or story. Secondary modes should support the primary activity instead of fragmenting the design.

A primary decomposition writes an [[Ideal]] as a finite intersection of [[Primary Ideal]]s. In a [[Noetherian Ring]], every ideal has such a decomposition.

Taking radicals of the primary components reveals the associated [[Prime Ideal]]s, while the primary components retain information analogous to prime powers. The construction generalizes unique prime-power decomposition from integers to broader commutative rings.

5758.title: Price Boundary
5758.heading: Price Boundary
5758.content:
A price boundary is a designed floor or ceiling that limits how far market prices can move. A guaranteed low export price and higher import price can create a channel within which players trade freely.

The channel prevents a seller or buyer from completely controlling access while preserving dynamic price discovery. Linking its bounds to item rarity or power lets the viable price range expand coherently with progression.

Together with [[Play]], goals, and rules, pretending is one of the source's essential elements of a [[Game]]. Entering the [[Magic Circle]] is the social commitment to maintain that shared pretense.

5776.title: Presheaf
5776.heading: Presheaf
5776.content:
A presheaf assigns an algebraic object to every open set and a restriction map whenever one open set is contained in another. Restrictions compose consistently and act as the identity when an open set is restricted to itself.

A [[Sheaf]] is a presheaf satisfying additional locality and gluing conditions. Presheaves organize information that varies over a space even before those conditions are imposed.

5779.title: Presentation Matrix
5779.heading: Presentation Matrix
5779.content:
A presentation matrix for a module M has columns that generate the [[Syzygy Module]] of a chosen generating set of M. It appears in an exact sequence Rˢ → Rᵗ → M → 0.

The matrix encodes relations among generators. Its minors define [[Fitting Ideal]]s, and its kernel supplies the next module in a free resolution.

5788.title: Presence
5788.heading: Presence
5788.content:
Presence is the feeling of being in a [[Virtual Environment]] rather than in the physical world. It is an important but incompletely understood part of [[User Experience]] in virtual systems.

Presence can be assessed through rating scales and questionnaires, responses to controlled changes in the environment, physiological reactions, behavior toward virtual events, memory, or performance on tasks that depend on feeling present. Each method captures only part of the concept, and there is no universally accepted single measure.

Display characteristics, natural movement, [[Spatial Audio]], consistent [[Feedback]], and interaction quality can all influence presence.

5791.title: Premise
5791.heading: Premise
5791.content:
Also known as an input to a logical system
A statement that can be either true or false

A premise is accepted as true for the purpose of an argument. Logical validity guarantees only that a [[Conclusion]] follows if the premises hold; it does not establish the factual truth of the premises themselves.

5794.title: Preliminary Knowledge
5794.heading: Preliminary Knowledge
5794.content:
Preliminary knowledge is the information a modeler contributes before learning from the current dataset. In Bayesian programming it includes the choice of variables, the decomposition of their joint distribution, and the mathematical forms assigned to the factors.

A prior over parameters is only one small part of this knowledge. Changing the variables or conditional-independence assumptions can alter the model more fundamentally than changing a numerical prior.

5797.title: Pregel
5797.heading: Pregel
5797.content:
Pregel is a distributed graph-processing model built around vertex-centric computation in synchronized supersteps. Each active vertex reads incoming messages, updates its state, and sends messages that become available in the next superstep.

Global barriers simplify reasoning and checkpointing but allow a slow or overloaded worker to delay every other partition.

5803.content:
A predictor variable is an observed or derived quantity used to explain or predict an outcome. In a linear model it contributes one or more columns to the [[Design Matrix]], depending on whether it is numeric, categorical, transformed, or involved in an interaction.

The term does not imply causation. A predictor can improve fit because it represents a cause, a consequence, a confounder, or merely a correlated measurement.

5806.title: Predictive Policing Feedback Loop
5806.heading: Predictive Policing Feedback Loop
5806.content:
A predictive policing feedback loop occurs when recorded police activity is used to direct future enforcement, causing more activity to be recorded in the same places and then treated as evidence of greater underlying crime. The model learns partly from the institution's earlier attention rather than from a neutral measure of all offending.

This loop can intensify unequal surveillance even if the algorithm applies its rule consistently. More deployment creates more data, and more data appear to validate the deployment. Breaking the loop requires distinguishing reported or discovered incidents from actual prevalence and evaluating the social costs of concentrated enforcement.

5809.heading: Predictive Feature Relevance
5809.content:
Predictive feature relevance is the degree to which a variable helps distinguish observations belonging to different classes. With labels available, relevance can be estimated through association, dependence, distance, or class-separation criteria.

A relevant feature contributes information about the target rather than merely varying across cases. The source emphasizes that selecting discriminative features can improve generalization, reduce computation and storage, and leave the original variables interpretable.

In the book's workflow, relevance is examined alongside redundancy and operational availability. A highly ranked field can still be unsuitable if it is an identifier, leaks the target, is mostly missing, or cannot be obtained when predictions are made.

5812.title: Predicate Logic
5812.heading: Predicate Logic
5812.content:
Predicate logic extends [[Propositional Logic]] by representing properties and relations that become propositions when applied to entities. A one-place predicate P associates each entity in its domain of discourse with the proposition P(a), while predicates with several places express relations among several entities.

Variables in an open statement remain free until a [[Universal Quantifier]] or [[Existential Quantifier]] binds them. This lets logic express general claims that propositional variables alone cannot preserve.

5815.title: Prediction
5815.heading: Prediction
5815.content:
Prediction propagates a current belief through a state transition model to estimate a future hidden state. The farther the requested state lies beyond the latest observation, the more transition uncertainty can accumulate.

In the generic Bayesian filter, prediction is the question whose searched state has a positive temporal offset from the last known evidence. It can be followed by correction when a new observation arrives.

5827.title: Precision
5827.heading: Precision
5827.content:
Precision is the proportion of predicted positive cases that are truly positive. It answers how reliable a positive prediction is and falls when false positives increase.

Precision depends on the selected threshold and class prevalence, so it should be interpreted alongside [[Recall]] and the operational cost of false alarms.

5830.title: Precision Medicine
5830.heading: Precision Medicine
5830.content:
Precision medicine adapts prevention, diagnosis, or treatment to characteristics of an individual or biologically meaningful subgroup. Genomic variation can be combined with clinical and environmental information to estimate risk or likely treatment response.

The promise depends on representative evidence, validated associations, interpretable decisions, privacy protections, and clinical context rather than sequence volume alone.

5842.title: Poynting Vector
5842.heading: Poynting Vector
5842.content:
The Poynting vector is the cross product of electric and magnetic field intensity and represents electromagnetic power density and flow direction. Integrating its normal component over a surface gives power crossing that surface.

For time-harmonic fields, the real part of a complex field product gives average power. Poynting's theorem balances radiated power, stored field energy, and resistive dissipation.

5845.title: PowerGraph
5845.heading: PowerGraph
5845.content:
PowerGraph is a distributed graph system designed for natural graphs with highly skewed degree distributions. It uses vertex cuts so edges can be balanced among machines while high-degree vertices are replicated across their partitions.

The gather-apply-scatter abstraction coordinates local edge contributions with a master copy of each replicated vertex.

5848.title: Power
5848.heading: Power
5848.content:
A power is an expression (a^n) formed from a [[Base of a Power]] and an [[Exponent]]. For positive integer (n), its value is the product of (n) copies of (a).

The second and third powers have special names: a [[Square]] and a [[Cube]]. Powers compress repeated structure and make patterns such as growth in a [[Geometric Progression]] easy to express. They follow the [[Laws of Exponents]], which permit products, quotients, and nested powers to be simplified without expanding every repeated factor.

5854.title: Power Set
5854.heading: Power Set
5854.content:
The power set P(A) is the set of every [[Subset]] of A. It always contains the empty set and A itself; if A is finite with n elements, then P(A) has 2^n elements.

Power sets distinguish membership from containment: ∅ is a subset of every set and therefore an element of every power set. Cantor's result that no set is bijective with its power set also drives the distinction between countable and [[Uncountable Set|uncountable sets]].

5857.heading: Power Sensitivity Analysis
5857.content:
A power sensitivity analysis repeats a power or sample-size calculation across a range of plausible effect sizes. It shows how strongly the design requirement depends on an uncertain assumption instead of presenting one number with false precision.

The sequence should remain within values that the statistical function can evaluate and that the science can defend. Automation can calculate every scenario, but the resulting curve or table still needs an explanation of which effects would be practically meaningful.

5860.title: Power Rule
5860.heading: Power Rule
5860.content:
The power rule states

$$\frac{d}{dx}x^n=nx^{n-1}.$$

For positive integers it follows from expanding the difference quotient, and the rule extends to rational powers wherever the corresponding real function is differentiable. Combined with the sum rule, it differentiates any [[Polynomial]] term by term.

5866.title: Power Method
5866.heading: Power Method
5866.content:
The power method starts with a [[Vector]] and repeatedly multiplies it by the same [[Matrix]]. Under the required conditions, the successive vectors converge toward the matrix's leading [[Eigenvector]].

PageRank begins with relative-importance values summing to one and repeatedly applies the Google matrix. When another iteration no longer changes the [[PageRank Vector]], the stable values provide the final ranking.

For a general matrix, each multiplication is normally followed by normalization to prevent overflow and expose the scale factor. Convergence requires a [[Dominant Eigenvalue]] and a starting vector with a nonzero component in its eigendirection; the [[Rayleigh Quotient]] can estimate the corresponding eigenvalue.

5869.heading: Potential Flow Finite Element Procedure
5869.content:
The potential-flow finite element procedure selects a scalar potential and element type, defines gradient-to-velocity relationships, derives element equations, and assembles a global system with boundary conditions.

The solved nodal potentials are differentiated to obtain element velocities and volumetric rates. This sequence mirrors structural FEM while replacing displacement and force with flow-specific field quantities.

5872.title: Potential Flow
5872.heading: Potential Flow
5872.content:
Potential flow is an irrotational flow of an ideal incompressible fluid. It can be formulated with a velocity potential or a stream function, chosen partly according to how easily boundary conditions can be imposed.

Finite element potential flow solves nodal scalar values and differentiates the field to recover velocity and volumetric rates. Flow around a cylinder or airfoil provides representative applications.

5875.title: Posthumanism
5875.heading: Posthumanism
5875.content:
Posthumanism questions the assumption that human beings are the central measure of intelligence, agency, and moral value. In AI ethics, it resists judging every nonhuman system only by how closely it imitates human thought or behavior.

This perspective can make room for unfamiliar forms of agency and for the interests of animals, ecosystems, and other nonhumans. It also emphasizes that people are already constituted through relationships with technologies. However, dissolving a sharp human-machine boundary must not obscure domination or exploitation. Power still determines whose interests are represented when a system is designed and whose lives bear its costs.

5878.title: Posterior Probability
5878.heading: Posterior Probability
5878.content:
Posterior probability is the distribution obtained after conditioning a model on observed evidence. It combines the prior description with the evidence likelihood and normalization required by the complete set of alternatives.

The posterior is conditional on both the observations and the modeling assumptions. It can answer the current question directly or become summarized knowledge used as a prior in a later recursive update.

5881.content:
Post-von-Neumann computational models seek alternatives to a processor repeatedly fetching instructions from separate memory. Quantum, neural, reversible, DNA, and memristive systems exploit different physical processes and favor different classes of problems.

Each architecture demands its own computational thinking. A representation natural for one machine may be awkward or meaningless for another, so architecture selection becomes part of problem formulation.

5884.heading: Possible Worlds Clustering
5884.content:
Possible-worlds clustering treats an uncertain dataset as a distribution over deterministic realizations. A clustering property is evaluated across those worlds, allowing probabilities or expected qualities to reflect alternative values.

The semantics are direct but exact enumeration is usually infeasible because worlds multiply across uncertain objects. Sampling, bounding, or analytic expectations approximate the distribution and introduce their own accuracy-cost tradeoffs.

5887.title: Possibility Space
5887.heading: Possibility Space
5887.content:
A possibility space is the set of actions, choices, strategies, and outcomes that a game's rules make available. Its boundaries come from the [[Game Verb|verbs]], objects, relationships, and constraints designed into the system.

The space may be narrow at one moment and wide at another. Rich possibility does not require unrestricted action; a compact set of strongly interacting rules can create more meaningful variety than a large set of unrelated options.
